lesson.title: Reading Reaction Order Off a Graph
lesson.summary: Shows how plotting the same concentration-time data three different ways reveals a reaction's order, since only the correct transformation produces a straight line.
lesson.body:
In a real experiment, you rarely know a reaction's order in advance. You determine it from data, and the most reliable way to do that is graphical: transform your measured concentrations in a few different standard ways and see which transformation produces a straight line. This works because of exactly the structural fact noticed in the last two sections. A plot of ln[A] versus t is a straight line only for a first order reaction, with slope -k. A plot of 1/[A] versus t is a straight line only for a second order reaction, with slope +k. A plot of [A] versus t itself is a straight line only for a zero order reaction, with slope -k. Human eyes, and simple statistical tools like linear regression, are very good at recognizing a straight line and quite bad at telling apart different families of curves by sight alone, which is exactly why chemists lean on this straight-line test rather than trying to eyeball a raw, curved plot.

The method in practice: collect [A] at several values of t, then compute ln[A] and 1/[A] for each data point alongside the raw [A]. Plot all three transformed versions against t. Whichever one comes out as a straight line tells you the order, and the slope of that particular line hands you the rate constant k directly, with the appropriate sign.

Worked example, using the same reaction from the first order sections of this unit, k = 0.0231 min^-1 and [A]0 = 0.500 M:

t (min): 0, 30, 60, 90
[A] (M): 0.500, 0.250, 0.125, 0.0625
ln[A]: -0.693, -1.386, -2.079, -2.773
1/[A] (M^-1): 2.00, 4.00, 8.00, 16.0

Look at the ln[A] column first. The differences between consecutive values are -0.693, -0.693, and -0.693, exactly evenly spaced across equal 30-minute intervals. Evenly spaced values, plotted against evenly spaced time points, is precisely what a straight line looks like. Computing the slope from the endpoints confirms it: slope = (-2.773 - (-0.693)) / (90 - 0) = -2.080 / 90 = -0.0231 min^-1, recovering the exact k value used to build this dataset in the first place.

Now look at the 1/[A] column for contrast. The differences are 2.00, 4.00, and 8.00, doubling each interval rather than staying constant. That is not a straight line, it is a curve, so this same dataset immediately rules out second order kinetics. Only one of the three transformations produced a straight line here, and that is exactly the diagnostic power of this method: it does not just confirm one hypothesis, it actively rules out the others using the same table of numbers.

This graphical test is the actual method used in real kinetics laboratories, not just a textbook exercise. The next two sections dig further into what the raw, untransformed concentration-time curve actually looks like for each order and why the algebra of the transformation works the way it does, building directly on the straight-line logic introduced here.
